proof:
If an active plane $B$ vanishes at a sampled point, its continuous coefficient is nonzero, since otherwise the entire fiber at that base would have parameter zero. Cut every fiber by $B\ge t$ for small positive $t$. The cut fibers are positive and satisfy anchored inclusions, since the inequality is affine on full mixed space. The mixed removed set $R_t$ has mass $a_t>0$ by the cone from the zero point to an interior ball, and $a_t\to0$ since the zero level is volume-null in every sampled fiber. With $h_t=a_t|\log t|$, $L\le B<t$ on $R_t$ gives $\int_{R_t}\log L\,dm\le-h_t$. Thus $h_t\to0$ by integrability and $a_t=o(h_t)$.

Write $\beta=Q/M$. For each of the $m$ old atomic caps take a nonnegative convex base hinge positive on its sampled trace and zero elsewhere, by translating its threshold downward by less than the smallest excluded-base gap and taking the positive part. Normalize each by its total boundary integral on the cut family and sum the normalized hinges. Their coefficients stay bounded because each cap has positive old mass, its cut fibers converge in Hausdorff distance to the old fibers, and their surface areas converge. Erode each cut fiber by duration $s$ times the summed rate at its base. Compatibility follows by the convexity of that rate and the inner parallel inclusion in 2fe966187abc0788. The total first loss is $m$ and each cap catches at least its own unit first loss. These first variations are uniform as $t,s\to0$: integrate the surface areas of the inner parallel fibers over the erosion interval. The bounded rates and the common inballs give uniform Hausdorff convergence of those fibers to the old ones throughout this interval, so their surface areas converge uniformly, with endpoint counting if $d=1$. With $s_t=C_0a_t$ and a fixed $C_0$ satisfying $C_0(1-\beta m)>\beta$, the final raw mass of each old covering cap minus $\beta$ times the final mass is bounded above by
$$
\beta a_t-s_t(1-\beta m)+o(s_t)<0 .
$$
This uses that the cut cap mass is at most $Q$. The hinge removes a further disjoint set $D_t$ of mass $d_t=O(a_t)$. For $m=0$ omit the hinge and take $D_t=\varnothing$ and $d_t=0$.

The exact final log normalization multiplier for the old raw $L$ on the final family is
$$
\log c_t=\frac{\int_{R_t}\log L\,dm+\int_{D_t}\log L\,dm}{M-a_t-d_t}
\le \frac{-h_t+O(a_t)}{M-a_t-d_t} .
$$
Here the second integral is bounded above by $d_t\max(0,\log\max_C L)$, including when other zero faces persist. The final hull is nested, so by d90ba05577427854 the energy at each retained mark can only fall. All removed mass is $O(a_t)$ and the old bodies are bounded and positive. Thus the total mass and pooled covariance factors change the physical buffer by at most $1+O(a_t)$, uniformly over all normals. The displayed log multiplier makes the final shift at most $(1-c h_t)$ times the old shift for some $c>0$ and small $t$, using the power $1/N$. A zero old boundary shift stays zero.

For each old proper deepest mark choose a fixed small own-interior neighborhood. There the old shifts are bounded below for Euclidean unit continuous normals, and by continuity the strict old atomic gap persists. Apply the compact representative and positive own-strip bound of 20210aa9d661295a on the closure of the chosen neighborhood. Uniformity follows by compactness of the marks and minimizing representatives and the strictly proper own traces. Raising the old cap threshold by a small constant times $h_t$ removes at least $c' h_t$ of own volume there. This comparison uses the old fiber slab, then uses nesting of the actual final bodies. Thus each retained proper neighborhood has final depth at most $Q-c'h_t$. Elsewhere on its base, and at all old nondeepest bases, compactness gives an old fixed gap and nesting with smaller buffers preserves it in raw depth. Division by the final mass costs only $O(a_t)$, which is $o(h_t)$. The atomic caps have already been put strictly below $\beta$ in normalized mass, so all sampled marks have a uniformly strict normalized upper bound below $\beta$. This contradicts the attained minimum. A zero on the canonical hull would force an affine constituent to have a sampled zero, by affinity and nonnegativity. Thus the finite-plane parameter is strictly positive on $C$.

statement:
Let $P$ be a finite nonempty complete base in an affine lattice, with positive compact convex $d$-fibers $K_z$ ($d\ge1$) satisfying the anchored Minkowski inclusions $\sum_z\lambda_z K_z\subseteq K_p$ whenever $\lambda_z\ge0$, $\sum_z\lambda_z=1$, and $\sum_z\lambda_z z=p\in P$. Put $S=\bigcup_z\{z\}\times K_z$, $C=\operatorname{conv}S$, $dm=\sum_z\delta_z\otimes dX|_{K_z}$ and $M=m(S)$. All affine functions are relative to $\operatorname{aff}P\times\mathbb R^d$. Let $\varepsilon>0$, $N=d+1$, and $G(u)=(M^{-1}\sum_z\int_{K_z}[u\cdot(X-g_z)]^2\,dX)^{1/2}$, where $g_z$ are the fiber centroids. Use marked energy $E_K(y)=\inf_a\int_K[1+a\cdot(X-y)]^{-d-1}\,dX$ over denominators strictly positive throughout $K$, extended by zero on $\partial K$. For a parameter $L$ put $f(z,y)=[L(z,y)E_{K_z}(y)/M]^{1/N}$ and use the infimum $b_L(p,y)$ of mixed masses of the caps
$$
a\cdot(z-p)+u\cdot(X-y)\ge-\varepsilon G(u)f(p,y),\qquad u\ne0,
$$
and of closed pure-base caps containing $p$ (including the whole-base trace). Write $b_{\rm base}(p)$ for the latter minimum alone. Let $Q=\max_S b_L$, $I$ be the bases of maximizing marks, $J=\{p\in I:b_{\rm base}(p)>Q\}$, $A=I\setminus J$, and $k(T)$ count inherited lattice parities occupied by $T$, with $k(\varnothing)=0$.

Assume $L$ is finite nonnegative upper-semicontinuous concave on $C$, positive on every sampled own interior, with $M^{-1}\int_S\log L\,dm=0$. The pair is an attained global minimizer of $Q/M$ at fixed $\varepsilon$ in this enlarged class of compatible positive families and log-normalized parameters, with $0<Q/M<1/k(P)$. At each proper deepest base assume one own-interior maximizing mark. Assume the atomic deepest bases admit a cover by $m$ old closed pure-base caps of mass $Q$, with $(Q/M)m<1$; take $m=0$ when $A=\varnothing$.

Suppose the minimizing parameter is the minimum of finitely many nonnegative affine planes. Then it is strictly positive on $C$.
title: A zero-face cut with simultaneous atomic cleanup
